steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper presenting BAN-PL, a Polish dataset of banned harmful and offensive content from the Wykop.pl service. Explain why such data is hard to obtain, especially for Polish, describe the source platform and its moderation, and say what the paper covers.

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Offensive language is everywhere on the Internet, so managing automated online content moderation well is a very important goal for NLP experts. But the main challenge is still getting accurate datasets, and this is complicated because such data cannot be represented synthetically. Cyberbullies use a wide spectrum of linguistic inventiveness, together with fractured syntax, so you would need at least a large language model to generate offensive samples that are convincing linguistically. But exactly these models block this kind of content, which makes it hardly possible to analyze or create it. So training data has to be gathered from the flood of new content that is posted online every day. However, finding a source that is reliable and representative is still a major issue, especially for low-resource languages.

In recent years the availability of resources has grown a lot, for example the Catalog of Abusive Language Data includes 25 languages, but resources for offensive content have developed unevenly, and there is only one entry listed for the Polish language.

In this paper we introduce BAN-PL, which is a Polish language dataset of banned offensive content, to fill this gap in available resources. It is one of the few publicly available datasets that has content reported by community members (in this case users of the service Wykop.pl), which was identified as offensive and then deleted by professional content moderators.

- Wykop.pl
  - established December 2005, equivalent of digg.com; "Polish Reddit"
  - among top 10 most popular SNS in Poland; ~3 million real users as of February 2023; ~30,000 new posts and comments daily
  - trained moderators from the community; any user can flag content, taxonomy of over 20 ban reasons
  - flagged content reviewed by moderator: approved or removed
- This paper
  - dataset + analysis of key linguistic features; insights into real-life moderation
  - comprehensive anonymization beyond usernames and URLs
  - biases: post-moderation, pre-selection (see 6)

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Offensive language is everywhere on the Internet, so managing automated online content moderation well is a very important goal for NLP experts. But the main challenge is still getting accurate datasets, and this is complicated because such data cannot be represented synthetically. Cyberbullies use a wide spectrum of linguistic inventiveness, together with fractured syntax, so you would need at least a large language model to generate offensive samples that are convincing linguistically. But exactly these models block this kind of content, which makes it hardly possible to analyze or create it. So training data has to be gathered from the flood of new content that is posted online every day. However, finding a source that is reliable and representative is still a major issue, especially for low-resource languages.

In recent years the availability of resources has grown a lot, for example the Catalog of Abusive Language Data includes 25 languages, but resources for offensive content have developed unevenly, and there is only one entry listed for the Polish language.

In this paper we introduce BAN-PL, which is a Polish language dataset of banned offensive content, to fill this gap in available resources. It is one of the few publicly available datasets that has content reported by community members (in this case users of the service Wykop.pl), which was identified as offensive and then deleted by professional content moderators.

Wykop.pl was set up in December 2005 as an equivalent of the digg.com web service. It is often called the Polish Reddit, and it is currently listed as one of the top 10 most popular social networking services (SNS) in Poland, with about 3 million real users as of February 2023. These users write around 30,000 new posts and comments every day. The content is constantly monitored by trained moderators from the user community. Also, every user can flag any piece of content on their own, using an internal taxonomy of over 20 different ban reasons. If users flag some content, a moderator has to review it and either approve it as non-harmful or remove it from the website.

Apart from introducing a new dataset and analyzing its most important linguistic features and characteristics, the paper also gives useful insights into how content moderation works in real life. We also describe and apply a comprehensive anonymization procedure, which goes further than the usual masking of usernames and URLs. Finally we discuss the common biases found in similar datasets, including post-moderation and pre-selection biases (see 6).

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Given the pervasive nature of offensive language on the Internet, effectively managing automated online content moderation is a paramount objective for NLP experts. However, the main challenge remains the accessibility of accurate datasets, which is complicated by the inability to represent them synthetically. The wide spectrum of linguistic inventiveness used by cyberbullies, combined with fractured syntax, requires at least a large language model to generate linguistically convincing offensive samples. Yet exactly these models block such content, making it hardly possible to analyze or create it ([1]). Training data should therefore be gathered from the daily flood of new content posted online. However, finding a reliable and representative source is still a major issue, especially for low-resource languages.

Although the availability of resources has grown significantly in recent years, with the Catalog of Abusive Language Data including 25 languages ([2]), the development of resources for offensive content has been uneven, with only one entry listed for the Polish language.

In this paper, we introduce BAN-PL, a Polish language dataset of banned offensive content, to address this gap in available resources. Notably, it is one of the few publicly available datasets ([3]) containing content reported by community members (here, users of the service Wykop.pl), identified as offensive, and subsequently deleted by professional content moderators.

Wykop.pl was established in December 2005 as an equivalent to the digg.com web service ([4]). Often called the Polish Reddit ([5]), it is currently listed as one of the top 10 most popular social networking services (SNS) in Poland, with approximately 3 million real users as of February 2023, who generate around 30,000 new posts and comments daily ([6]). The content is constantly monitored by trained moderators from the user community. In addition, every user can independently flag any piece of content using an internal taxonomy of over 20 different ban reasons. Flagged content must be reviewed by a moderator, who either approves it as non-harmful or removes it from the website.

Besides introducing a new dataset and analyzing its most critical linguistic features and characteristics, the paper also provides valuable insights into real-life content moderation processes. Furthermore, we describe and apply a comprehensive anonymization procedure that goes beyond the typical masking of usernames and URLs. The prevalent biases found in similar datasets, including post-moderation and pre-selection biases (see 6), are also discussed.
